title: Overview
text: # Overview AI Engineering Platform is a workspace where AI agents execute the software lifecycle and people keep the decisions that matter. A task moves through a defined path: 1. **Shape** — a project blueprint creates the workspace; a task gets a description and acceptance criteria. 2. **Plan** — the planning agent proposes steps, files and risks against a frozen context. 3. **Approve** — a human approves the plan before code is written. 4. **Build** — a development agent works in a disposable sandbox and produces a diff. 5. **Prove** — tests, design checks and acceptance evidence are recorded. 6. **Review** — a pull request is opened; a human approves the merge. 7. **Learn** — delivery and quality metrics show what happened. The platform does not hide these steps behind a chat box. Every transition is an event with an actor, an artifact and a timestamp. ![Workspace overview](../../assets/product-overview.png) *The workspace: health, projects and the next setup step.* ## Who it is for | Team | What they use it for | |---|---| | Product and platform teams | Repeatable delivery with approvals and an audit trail | | Agencies and studios | One workspace per client, with project-level access | | Regulated teams | Human gates, isolation and exportable audit evidence | ## What you need - A workspace (organisation) and a project. - A Git provider connection: GitHub App, GitLab, or a token for local development. - A model provider or a registered agent plugin. - A sandbox runtime (Docker locally, Kubernetes for a cluster deployment). ## Principles - **Plan before code.** A task cannot start without a definition of ready. - **Sandbox everything.** The agent cannot touch the host, the network or another run. - **Prove acceptance.** The diff must carry evidence for every acceptance criterion. - **Humans merge.** No agent merges its own pull request. - **Measure outcomes.** Speed is reported next to rework, proof validity and escaped defects. ## Where to go next - [Quickstart](quickstart.html) — run the platform locally and complete one task. - [Key concepts](concepts.html) — the lifecycle, gates and roles. - [Tasks and board](tasks-and-board.html) — how work is shaped. - [API reference](../api.html) — every REST endpoint.

title: Quickstart
text: # Quickstart This guide runs the platform on one machine with Docker Compose. It is the fastest path to a first approved, merged task. ## Prerequisites - Docker 27+ with Compose v2 - `make`, `git`, `go` and `node` for development commands - 8 GB RAM available to Docker (16 GB recommended for the full stack) ## 1. Start the local stack ```bash cp .env.example .env make keygen docker compose up -d postgres redis minio mailhog make dev ``` The API starts on `http://localhost:18080`, the web app on `http://localhost:3000`, and MinIO on `http://localhost:9001`. Check the health endpoints: ```bash curl -sf http://localhost:18080/readyz curl -sf http://localhost:3000/login >/dev/null && echo web-ok ``` ## 2. Sign in Open `http://localhost:3000`, sign in with the demo account seeded by the local environment, and select your workspace. If you are starting from an empty database, create an account from the register screen and follow the setup checklist on the overview. ## 3. Create a project from a blueprint 1. Open **Blueprints**. 2. Pick a template or create a blueprint version. 3. Publish the version. 4. Open **Projects → New project** and instantiate the blueprint. 5. Connect the repository and choose the agent/model allowed for the project. A project created from a blueprint already has the stack, test strategy, design rules, agents and starter tasks. ## 4. Create a task 1. Open the project and choose **Board**. 2. Select **+ New task**. 3. Write the outcome, context and at least one acceptance criterion in Given/When/Then form. 4. Move the task from **Draft** to **Ready** once the definition of ready is satisfied. ![New task drawer](../../assets/product-new-task.png) *The task drawer: context, acceptance criteria and design references before an agent starts.* ## 5. Run the planning agent On a ready task, choose **Run agent → planning**. The run view shows the context snapshot, the plan and every event. The run stops at **awaiting approval**. Approve the plan if it is correct; request changes or reject it otherwise. Nothing is implemented before this gate. ## 6. Build, test and review Approve the plan, then start the development run. The agent works in a sandbox; the platform records the diff, tests, design checks and acceptance evidence. A pull request is opened when the work is ready. Review the diff and the checks, then approve the PR. The merge queue serialises the landing; no agent can merge its own change. ## 7. Read the outcome Open **Analytics** to see lead time, approval time, first-pass merge, proof validity and rework for the period. Open the run or the audit log to inspect the evidence behind a number. ![Analytics](../../assets/product-analytics.png) *Delivery and outcome metrics are recorded from real runs, not estimated.* ## Stop and reset ```bash make down # remove local state only when you mean it: docker compose down -v ``` ## Next - [Key concepts](concepts.html) - [Runs and approvals](runs-and-approvals.html) - [API basics](api-basics.html)

title: Key concepts
text: # Key concepts The platform implements an **AI Software Development Lifecycle (ASDLC)**: a sequence of phases, artifacts and gates. The model is replaceable; the process is the product. ## Lifecycle at a glance ``` idea → blueprint → backlog → ready → plan → approve → build → test → review → PR approval → merge → measure ``` Each arrow is a state transition. The platform records who or what caused it. ## Phases | Phase | Owner | Output | |---|---|---| | Blueprint | human + agent | project template: stack, repository layout, tests, agents | | Backlog | human | tasks with context and acceptance criteria | | Definition of ready | human | a task that can safely start | | Plan | planning agent | steps, files, risks, estimated cost | | Build | development agent | a diff in an isolated sandbox | | Test | agent + platform | test report, design checks, acceptance evidence | | Review | human + agent | findings, PR comments, approval or rejection | | Merge | human | a merged change in the Git provider | | Measure | platform | delivery and quality metrics | ## Gates A gate is a deliberate stop. It cannot be skipped silently; an explicit override is recorded as an event. 1. **Plan approval** — a human accepts the plan before implementation. 2. **Test gate** — required checks must pass; acceptance evidence must be valid. 3. **Design gate** — design standards and visual checks for UI changes. 4. **PR approval** — a human approves the pull request. 5. **Merge queue** — changes land in a serialised order. ## Artifacts Every artifact is versioned and hashed: - **context manifest** — the exact files, rules and token budget given to the agent - **plan** — steps, files, risks and cost estimate - **diff** — the change produced by the run - **test report** — unit, integration, e2e and visual results - **review** — findings and their severity - **audit event** — append-only record of a decision or transition ## Roles | Role | Typical responsibilities | |---|---| | Owner | workspace billing, members, security settings | | Admin | projects, providers, rules, integrations, audit | | Member | tasks, runs, reviews, pull requests | | Viewer | read-only access to projects and results | Roles are enforced by the API and the UI; project-level access can be narrower than the workspace role. ## Runs A run is one agent execution with a type: **planning**, **development** or **review**. Runs are resumable at phase boundaries and stop at approvals. A run has a budget, a frozen context and an append-only event stream. ## Two kinds of speed The platform reports delivery speed **and** outcome quality: - lead time and approval time - first-pass merge and proof validity - rework, change failure rate and escaped defects A faster merge that creates more rework is not an improvement. ## Next - [Projects and blueprints](projects-blueprints.html) - [Runs and approvals](runs-and-approvals.html) - [Quality gates](quality.html)

title: Projects and blueprints
text: # Projects and blueprints A **blueprint** is the only entry point for creating a project. It captures the decisions that should not be reinvented for every repository. ## What a blueprint contains - stack and repository layout - test strategy and required checks - design standards and component registry references - default agents and allowed models - starter tasks and acceptance templates - project rules and approval requirements ![Blueprints](../../assets/product-blueprints.png) *Published templates and versioned project blueprints.* ## Create a blueprint version 1. Open **Blueprints**. 2. Choose a template or **+ New blueprint**. 3. Edit the definition: stack, test strategy, agents, rules. 4. Save a version. Versions are immutable. 5. Review the diff and **Publish**. A published version can be instantiated by projects. Draft versions are visible only to the team. ## Create a project 1. Open **Projects → New project**. 2. Name the project and select the blueprint version. 3. Connect the Git repository: - install the GitHub App for the repository, or - connect a GitLab project, or - use a token for a local repository. 4. Choose the default branch and the agent/model allowed for the project. 5. Create the project. The project inherits the blueprint's test strategy, rules and starter tasks. You can override values per project, but the blueprint version used at creation is recorded. ## Repositories The **Repositories** view shows the connected repositories and their status. A repository must be reachable by the worker before a run can clone it. For GitHub, the App installation grants access to selected repositories. For GitLab, the connection is scoped to a project. Tokens are stored encrypted and never returned by the API. ## Project settings | Setting | Effect | |---|---| | Required checks | Checks that must be green before a PR can merge | | E2E command | Command run after unit tests in the sandbox | | Required approvals | Number of distinct approvers for a PR | | Merge window | Time window in which the merge queue may land changes | | MCP servers | Trusted tool servers available to runs | | Agents and models | Providers and agent plugins allowed in the project | ## Permissions - **Owner/Admin** can create, edit and archive projects and blueprints. - **Member** can work with tasks and runs in projects they can access. - **Viewer** can read the board, runs and results. ## Limits and good practice - Keep a blueprint small enough to review; put product-specific detail in tasks. - Publish a new version instead of editing a published one. - Connect only the repositories the project needs. - Use project-level rules when a client or repository needs stricter controls. ## Next - [Tasks and board](tasks-and-board.html) - [Agents and models](models-byok.html)

title: Tasks and board
text: # Tasks and board The board is the source of truth for what the team is doing. It is deliberately not a prompt box. ![Project board](../../assets/product-board.png) *Draft, Ready, Planning, In progress and Review columns. A card only moves when the transition is valid.* ## Columns | Column | Meaning | |---|---| | Draft | Incomplete idea; an agent cannot start | | Ready | Meets the definition of ready and can be planned | | Planning | A planning run is active or waiting for approval | | In progress | A development run has an approved plan | | Review | A pull request is open and checks are running | | Done | The change is merged and the task is closed | A blocked task leaves the flow and records a reason. A human decides how to unblock it; the agent does not guess. ## Definition of ready A task becomes **Ready** when all of these are true: - the title is an imperative sentence (`Add SSO login`, not `SSO`) - at least one acceptance criterion uses Given/When/Then - the affected area or packages are identified - what is out of scope is stated when scope creep is a risk - dependencies are listed, or explicitly none - the work is small enough for one agent run If a criterion is missing, the platform keeps the task in Draft. This is a feature, not friction. ## Create a task 1. Open the project and choose **Board**. 2. Select **+ New task**. 3. Write the outcome and context. Include constraints, links and current behaviour. 4. Add acceptance criteria. 5. Add design references or technical context. 6. Save as Draft. Move to Ready when the definition of ready is met. ![Task creation](../../assets/product-new-task.png) *The task drawer asks for acceptance criteria before it asks for a model.* ## Good task hygiene - One outcome per task. Split large work. - Write acceptance criteria as observable behaviour, not implementation steps. - Link the design or component when the change affects UI. - State what must not change; this prevents unrelated edits. - Keep the description current. The run freezes the context it received. ## Priorities and filters Tasks have a priority and labels. Use the board filters to focus on a project, a status or a priority. The API exposes the same filters for automation. ## Permissions - Members can create and edit tasks in accessible projects. - Viewers can read the board and task details. - Admins can configure the definition of ready and required approvals at project level. ## Next - [Agent runs](runs-and-approvals.html) - [Quality gates](quality.html)

title: Agent runs and approvals
text: # Agent runs and approvals A **run** is one agent execution. It has a type, a frozen context, a budget and an event stream. The run view is where a team sees what the agent did and decides what happens next. ![A completed run](../../assets/product-run.png) *A development run: plan, approval, build, test and review in one timeline, with the diff that will be merged.* ## Run types | Type | Purpose | Gate | |---|---|---| | Planning | Inspect context and propose steps, files and risks | Plan approval | | Development | Implement the approved plan and produce a diff | Test/design gates, PR approval | | Review | Inspect a diff and report findings | PR approval | ## Start a run 1. Open a **Ready** task. 2. Choose **Run agent** and select the type. 3. Confirm the model/agent and budget if the project allows a choice. 4. Watch the run view; events stream live. A run cannot start if the task is not ready, if the repository is unreachable, or if the project has no allowed agent. ## What the run view shows - **Context** — the frozen manifest: files, rules and token budget - **Plan** — steps, files, risks and estimated cost - **Approval** — the decision and who made it - **Changes** — the diff, with additions and deletions - **Checks** — tests, design checks and acceptance evidence - **Cost** — recorded tokens and provider cost - **Events** — an append-only timeline with timestamps ## Approvals ### Plan approval A human can **approve**, **request changes** or **reject**. - Approve sends the run to implementation. - Request changes returns it to planning with a note. - Reject stops the run and leaves the task for a human. The approval records the user, the time and the plan version. ### PR approval A pull request requires the configured number of distinct approvers and all required checks. An agent cannot approve its own PR or bypass branch protection. ## Retry, cancel and failures - **Retry** starts a new run from a checkpoint or from the beginning, depending on the failure. - **Cancel** is cooperative: the worker asks the runtime to stop and kills the sandbox. - A failed run keeps its events and artifacts for inspection. The task returns to a state a human can act on. Common failure reasons are shown in the run view: clone failure, provider error, budget exceeded, missing proof or a failed check. ## Budgets A run has a token and cost budget. The worker checks it between phases. When the budget is exhausted the run fails with a clear reason instead of continuing silently. ## Next - [Pull requests and merges](pull-requests.html) - [Quality gates](quality.html) - [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.html)

title: Pull requests and merges
text: # Pull requests and merges The platform opens a pull request when a development run is ready. The PR is the hand-off between the agent's diff and the team's repository rules. ![Pull requests and checks](../../assets/product-pull-requests.png) *Every PR shows its provider, number, status and required checks. The merge queue serialises landing.* ## What is checked Before a PR can merge: - required checks are green - the test gate passed and coverage did not drop beyond the project threshold - design checks passed for UI changes - acceptance evidence maps to every criterion - the required number of humans approved - the merge window allows landing A missing check is not a warning. The merge button stays unavailable. ## Reviewing a PR 1. Open the PR from the run or the project's **Delivery → Pull requests** view. 2. Read the diff and the run evidence. 3. Leave comments or request changes. 4. Approve when the change is correct. Approvals are distinct users. The author of the run cannot count as the approver when the project requires an independent review. ## Merge queue The merge queue lands approved changes in order. It exists to prevent two green PRs from breaking each other at the last moment. - A PR enters the queue after approval. - The queue rebases or re-runs required checks as configured. - If a check fails, the PR leaves the queue and returns to the author with the reason. ## Merge windows Admins can restrict landing to a time window. Outside the window, approved PRs wait; the queue shows the next allowed time. ## Failed checks A failed check keeps the PR open. Fix the cause, push a new commit and let the checks run again. Do not weaken a check to make it pass; change the code or the test. ## Provider differences GitHub and GitLab are supported, and the token that opens the PR is resolved per repository ([Git providers](git-providers.html)). Both providers can rebase a PR/MR before merge; GitLab's rebase is asynchronous and the queue waits for the conflict status before it merges. The provider is recorded on the repository and on each PR. Branch protection remains the final authority in the Git provider; the platform does not bypass it. ## Next - [Quality gates](quality.html) - [Analytics](analytics.html)

title: Git providers
text: # Git providers The platform talks to your repository host with a token. That token pushes branches, opens pull requests / merge requests, reads checks and (optionally) protects the default branch. This page explains which token is used, how to scope it, and what to check when the provider answers with an error. Everything here is about **outbound** calls from the platform to GitHub or GitLab. Inbound webhooks are covered in [Webhooks](#webhooks). ## How the platform chooses a token For every repository operation the platform tries the sources in this order and stops at the first one that yields a token: | # | Source | Scope | Where it is configured | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Repository credential | one repository | Project **Delivery → Repositories → Credential** (owner/admin) | | 2 | GitHub App installation token | every repo the app is installed on | **Settings → Integrations → GitHub App**, or `AIP_GITHUB_APP_*` | | 3 | Global provider token | every repo the token can see | `AIP_GITHUB_TOKEN` / `AIP_GITLAB_TOKEN` in `.env` | The first source that returns a non-empty token wins; a failure in one source falls through to the next, so a revoked repository credential does not stop delivery as long as an App or global token exists. The resolution order is evaluated per repository, not per project. > **Pilot recommendation:** give the pilot project its own fine-grained PAT as a > repository credential. The global token stays untouched for the rest of the > organisation. ## Per-repository credential A repository credential is a PAT or project access token stored encrypted with `AIP_SECRETS_KEY` (the same key that protects model provider keys). It is the narrowest and safest option: the token only has to see one repository. ![Repository credential panel](../../assets/product-repo-credential.png) *Project → Delivery → Repositories: the credential panel shows the repository, the token hint and when it was last updated — never the token.* ### Store a credential 1. Open the project, **Delivery → Repositories**. 2. Next to the repository, choose **Credential**. 3. Paste the token and **Save**. The panel then shows the last four characters (`…9f2c`) and the update time — never the token itself. 4. Run a development run, or use **Protect branch**, to confirm the token works. The same operation over the API: ```bash curl -s -X PUT "$AIP_API_URL/api/v1/orgs/$ORG/projects/$PROJECT/repos/$REPO/credential" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"token":"github_pat_..."}' ``` `GET` on the same path returns only the status: ```json { "configured": true, "hint": "…9f2c", "updated_at": "2026-11-15T20:10:00Z" } ``` `DELETE` removes the credential and the repository immediately falls back to the App or the global token. Removing a credential that is not there is a no-op. ### Rules - Only **owner** and **admin** can set or remove a credential; any member can read the status. - If `AIP_SECRETS_KEY` is not configured, writes fail with a validation error instead of storing a plaintext token. - Setting and removing a credential write an audit event (`repo.credential.set` / `repo.credential.deleted`) with the repo id and the hint. The token never appears in the audit log. - Replacing a credential is a new `PUT`; there is no separate rotation endpoint. ## GitHub fine-grained PAT Create the token under **Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens**. - **Repository access:** *Only select repositories* and pick the one repository. - **Permissions:** - *Contents*: read and write — push branches. - *Pull requests*: read and write — open and merge PRs. - *Checks*: read — read check runs for the gate. - *Metadata*: read — mandatory, granted automatically. - *Administration*: read and write — only required for **Protect branch** (branch protection and required checks). Skip it if your team manages branch protection outside the platform. - **Expiration:** prefer a short expiry. When it lapse

title: Quality gates
text: # Quality gates Quality is enforced by evidence, not by asking the agent to "be careful". ## The test ladder | Layer | What it proves | |---|---| | Unit | Logic and edge cases in isolation | | Integration | Boundaries: database, queue, object storage | | End-to-end | The user flow works through the real surfaces | | Visual | The UI matches the approved design baseline | | Security | No new secrets, vulnerable dependencies or forbidden changes | The project's test strategy defines which layers are required. The e2e command runs in the sandbox after unit tests; a failure blocks the PR. ## Acceptance evidence Every task has acceptance criteria. A development run must produce an `AIP_PROOF` artifact that maps evidence to each criterion: ``` criterion: user can sign in with SSO evidence: e2e/sso.spec.ts > signs in with SAML ``` The platform validates that the referenced test or file exists in the diff. A proof that points to a missing test fails the run. ## Design checks For UI changes the platform can compare a rendered screen against the project's baseline: - layout, spacing and typography - component usage from the design system - accessibility checks - visual diff threshold A visual difference does not approve or reject itself. It produces evidence for the human reviewer. ## Diff policy Project rules can block changes before review: - forbidden paths (secrets, generated files, infrastructure) - maximum diff size - dependency changes that need an ADR - missing migration for a schema change - new network calls in the sandbox ## Review findings A review run reports findings with severity. Findings are not automatically blocking unless the project says so; the PR approval remains the human gate. ## What to do when a gate fails 1. Read the failing check, not just the summary. 2. Reproduce locally with the same command. 3. Fix the cause, not the assertion. 4. Re-run the check or the agent run. 5. Record an override only when a human accepts the risk; the override is audited. ## Next - [Pull requests](pull-requests.html) - [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.html)

title: Analytics
text: # Analytics Analytics answers two questions: how fast is delivery, and is the quality improving? ![Analytics](../../assets/product-analytics.png) *Delivery and outcome metrics for the selected period.* ## Metrics | Metric | What it means | |---|---| | Lead time | From ready task to merged change | | Approval time | Time spent waiting for human decisions | | Onboarding | Time from project creation to the first accepted task | | Run success | Completed runs divided by all runs | | Cost per accepted change | Provider cost divided by merged changes | | First-pass merge | PRs merged without a rework cycle | | Proof validity | Acceptance proofs that referenced real evidence | | Runs per task | How much agent work a task needed | | Change failure rate | Merged changes that required a fix | | Escaped defects | Defects found after merge, per 100 merges | Metrics marked **measured** come from recorded events. Metrics marked **na** have no data yet; the platform does not invent a value. ## Filtering Use the period selector to compare delivery windows. Project filters narrow the view to one product or client. ## Reading the numbers - A short lead time with a high rework rate is not an improvement. - A high proof validity rate with a low first-pass merge rate suggests the plan or context needs work. - Approval time is often the largest lever; it is a human process metric, not an agent metric. ## Exports The API exposes the same analytics data. Use it for a dashboard or a weekly report. Large exports should page through the API rather than scrape the UI. ## Next - [Quality gates](quality.html) - [API reference](../api.html)

title: Users and access
text: # Users and access Workspace access is role-based and auditable. The same role model applies to the UI and the API. ## Roles | Role | Can | |---|---| | Owner | Manage members, workspace settings, security and workspace deletion | | Admin | Manage projects, blueprints, providers, integrations, rules and audit | | Member | Work with tasks, runs, reviews and pull requests in accessible projects | | Viewer | Read projects, runs, checks and metrics; cannot change state | Project access can be narrower than the workspace role. A member of the workspace does not automatically see every project. ## Invite a user 1. Open **Settings → Invites**. 2. Enter the email and choose a role. 3. Send the invite. 4. The user accepts it and joins the workspace. Pending invites can be revoked. The invite email is sent by the configured mailer (Mailhog locally, Postmark/SES in production). ## Members **Settings → Members** lists everyone in the workspace. Owners and admins can change a member's role or remove them. Removing a user revokes their sessions and API keys for that workspace. Their audit history remains. ## Single sign-on The platform supports OIDC and SAML: - **OIDC** — GitHub, Google, Keycloak or another provider - **SAML 2.0** — enterprise identity providers - **SCIM** — provision and deprovision users and groups from the identity provider SSO can be required for a workspace. When it is enforced, password login is disabled for members. ## API keys **Settings → API keys** creates a scoped key for automation. A key belongs to a user and inherits their workspace role; it can be revoked at any time. - Store the key in a secret manager. - Use one key per integration. - Rotate on a schedule and after a team change. - Never put a key in a task, a prompt or a repository. ## Sessions Users can sign out of the current session or all sessions. Revoking all sessions is the right action after a lost device or a role change. ## Next - [Security and audit](security-audit.html) - [API basics](api-basics.html)

title: Security and audit
text: # Security and audit The model is not the security boundary. The runtime, the approval gates and the audit trail are. ## Sandbox isolation Every agent run executes in a disposable container: - read-only root filesystem - writable workspace on tmpfs - all Linux capabilities dropped - no new privileges - no network by default; approved egress only - CPU, memory and process limits - host filesystem never mounted A run cannot read another run's workspace or the host's credentials. ## Code and data handling - Repository contents are cloned into the sandbox for the run. - Artifacts (plan, diff, test report, review) are stored in object storage and linked to the run. - Provider requests contain only the context the run needs; prompt content and secrets are not written to logs or telemetry. - Deleting a project removes its tasks, runs, repositories and incidents; audit records follow the retention policy. ## Audit trail ![Audit log](../../assets/product-audit.png) *Append-only audit events with export, legal hold and witness verification.* The audit log records security-relevant actions: - sign-in and sign-out - membership and role changes - approvals and overrides - provider, SSO, SCIM and API key changes - backup and restore requests - policy and rule changes Audit entries are append-only. Owners and admins can export NDJSON for a SIEM, place a legal hold, or verify the witness chain. ## Access controls - Workspace roles and project-level access - SSO enforcement and session revocation - scoped API keys - provider credentials encrypted at rest - BYOK envelope encryption for organisations that require their own key ## Reporting a concern Contact the workspace owner or the platform operator with the run ID, the timestamp and the affected project. Do not paste secrets or customer data into a ticket. ## Next - [Models and BYOK](models-byok.html) - [Backups and recovery](backups-recovery.html) - [API basics](api-basics.html)

title: Agents, models and BYOK
text: # Agents, models and BYOK The platform is model-agnostic. A project chooses which agents and providers it may use; the platform records the choice on every run. ## Supported execution modes | Mode | Use | |---|---| | Hosted provider | Anthropic or an OpenAI-compatible endpoint | | Command backend | A local or self-hosted agent command | | Custom agent plugin | A digest-pinned OCI image with a defined command | The provider and model are recorded on the run, together with token usage and cost. ## Configure a provider 1. Open **Settings → Providers**. 2. Add the provider and credentials. 3. Choose the default model for planning, development and review, or set it per project. 4. Test the connection. Credentials are encrypted and never shown again after saving. Rotate them from the same screen. ## Custom agent plugins A plugin is an OCI image pinned by digest: ```text ghcr.io/acme/agent@sha256:... ``` The worker runs the image's command only for the project and run types where the plugin is allowed. Signed images can be required; an unsigned image is rejected when cosign verification is on. ![Agent plugins](../../assets/product-agents.png) *Register a digest-pinned image, choose the run types and attach it to a project.* ## Bring your own key (BYOK) Organisations can supply their own KMS key for envelope encryption: 1. Open **Settings → Encryption**. 2. Add the KMS key and region. 3. Verify the key. 4. Enable BYOK for the workspace. Existing data uses data keys wrapped by the organisation key. Rotation re-wraps those keys in an operator-run job; verify the rotation runbook before changing the key. Revoking a key makes encrypted fields unreadable, so keep a recovery procedure. ## Regions A workspace has a region label. Requests routed to the wrong region are rejected with `421` when the regional guard is enabled. Multi-region data planes are an operator concern, not a per-task setting. ## MCP tools Projects can declare trusted MCP servers. The sandbox starts only the declared servers, with the project's allowlist. A tool that is not declared is unavailable to the run. ## Limits - A provider key is scoped to the workspace. - A plugin must be digest-pinned; tags are not accepted. - Model choices are constrained by the project's allowed list. - Budgets are enforced by the worker between phases. ## Next - [Runs and approvals](runs-and-approvals.html) - [Security and audit](security-audit.html)

title: Backups and recovery
text: # Backups and recovery Backups are a product surface for operators, not a cron job hidden on a server. ![Backups and DR](../../assets/product-backups.png) *WAL and base backup health, restore history, restore duration and the offsite mirror.* ## What is protected - **PostgreSQL** — WAL archiving plus periodic base backups - **Object storage** — artifacts and run evidence - **Configuration** — provider and workspace settings in the database - **Audit log** — append-only events with export and legal hold ## Health indicators The **Settings → Backups** panel shows: | Indicator | Meaning | |---|---| | WAL archive | Last archived segment and archive failures | | Last success | Age of the most recent successful archive | | Base backup | Name and age of the newest base backup | | Restores | Succeeded and failed restore requests | | Restore duration | Average time for a verified restore | | Offsite mirror | Age of the last successful offsite copy | Alerts fire when WAL archiving stops, a base backup is stale, a restore is too old or the offsite mirror is behind. ## Request a restore 1. Open **Settings → Backups**. 2. Choose a target time. It must be after the base backup and covered by archived WAL. 3. Select **Request restore**. 4. The restore worker claims the request, starts a scratch instance, replays WAL and verifies row counts. 5. The request shows **succeeded** with the target time and verified counts, or **failed** with the reason. A restore is a verification step, not a live cutover. Promoting the restored instance is an operator decision with its own runbook. ## Offsite The WAL and base backup buckets are mirrored to a second MinIO/S3 endpoint. An offsite restore drill proves the mirror is usable, not just present. ## Retention WAL and base backups have a configurable retention period (30 days in the reference deployment). Object storage lifecycle rules should match the retention policy; do not delete a base backup that a restore request may still need. ## What to test - restore to a timestamp before a known change - restore with the primary unavailable - restore from the offsite endpoint - alert when WAL archiving stops ## Limits - A restore cannot target a time before the oldest base backup. - A target after the last archived WAL is not recoverable; the wait is visible in the panel. - The scratch restore does not serve production traffic until promoted. ## Next - [Security and audit](security-audit.html) - [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.html)

title: Troubleshooting
text: # Troubleshooting Start with the run view and the event stream. Most failures have a specific event before the generic error. ## Sign-in | Symptom | Check | |---|---| | Redirect loop | Cookies blocked, wrong `AIP_WEB_URL`, or clock skew | | SSO button missing | OIDC/SAML not configured or enabled for the workspace | | 401 after login | Session expired or the API JWT key changed | | 403 on a project | Workspace role is insufficient or project access is narrower | | 401/403/404 from GitHub or GitLab | Token scope, SSO authorisation or repo access — see [Git providers](git-providers.html#troubleshooting) | ## A run will not start - The task is still **Draft**; complete the definition of ready. - The repository is unreachable; check the repository credential, the GitHub App installation or the GitLab connection ([Git providers](git-providers.html)). - The project has no allowed agent/model. - A previous active run exists for the task. ## A run failed Open the run and read the last events: - **clone failed** — repository access or branch name - **provider error** — credential, quota or model name - **budget exceeded** — raise the budget or split the task - **missing proof** — acceptance evidence does not map to a real test - **check failed** — read the failing test/check output, do not retry blindly Retry creates a new run; it does not erase the failed one. ## A PR is blocked - A required check is red. Open the check, not just the badge. - The approval count is not met. Approvals must be distinct users. - The merge window is closed. - The merge queue found a conflict or a failed re-check. ## A restore failed - The target is before the base backup or after the last archived WAL. - The object store credential expired. - The scratch volume still contains data; the runner cleans it before fetch. The request keeps the failure reason; do not delete it before recording the incident. ## Getting help Include the workspace, project, task or run ID, the timestamp and the exact error. Never include provider keys, tokens or customer data. ## Next - [Runs and approvals](runs-and-approvals.html) - [Backups and recovery](backups-recovery.html) - [API reference](../api.html)

title: SSE event catalog
text: # API · SSE event catalog `GET /api/v1/orgs/{org}/runs/{run}/events` ``` Content-Type: text/event-stream Cache-Control: no-cache X-Accel-Buffering: no ``` ## Protocol ``` id: 41 event: phase.completed data: {"run_id":"7c9e","phase":"implement","duration_ms":142300,"ts":"2026-10-21T18:22:09Z"} : ping ``` - `id` = `run_events.seq` (increases monotonically per run). On reconnect the client sends `Last-Event-ID`; the server first backfills from the database, then subscribes to Redis. - An unknown event type is **ignored** (forward compatibility). - Heartbeat `: ping` every 15s. The server closes the connection after 1h; the client reconnects. - `retry: 3000` is sent at the start of the stream. - If `Last-Event-ID` does not exist in the database (archived), the server sends `event: stream.reset` with `{"from_seq": N}` and continues from the oldest available. ## Types | `event` | When | `data` (key fields) | |---|---|---| | `run.queued` | run created | `run_id`, `agent_type`, `model` | | `run.started` | worker picked it up | `started_at` | | `phase.started` | entering a phase | `phase`, `attempt` | | `phase.completed` | leaving a phase | `phase`, `duration_ms`, `meta` | | `phase.failed` | phase failed | `phase`, `code`, `detail` | | `llm.started` | before the LLM call | `model`, `prompt_tokens_est` | | `llm.chunk` | token stream | `text` (delta), `index` | | `llm.completed` | end of the call | `tokens_in`, `tokens_out`, `cost_micros`, `finish_reason` | | `tool.call` | tool call | `tool`, `args_digest`, `permitted` | | `tool.result` | result | `tool`, `ok`, `duration_ms`, `bytes` | | `file.changed` | FS change in the sandbox | `path`, `change` (`added`/`modified`/`deleted`) | | `plan.ready` | plan ready for approval | `artifact_id`, `sha256`, `summary` | | `approval.requested` | waiting for a human | `approval_id`, `type` | | `approval.decided` | decision | `approval_id`, `status`, `decided_by` | | `test.started` / `test.completed` | test run | `suite`, `passed`, `failed`, `coverage_pct` | | `diff.ready` | diff finalized | `artifact_id`, `files`, `additions`, `deletions` | | `usage.updated` | after every LLM call | `tokens_in`, `tokens_out`, `cost_micros`, `budget_pct` | | `run.succeeded` | end | `duration_ms`, `head_commit`, `pr_url?` | | `run.failed` | end | `code`, `detail`, `retryable` | | `run.canceled` | cancellation | `requested_by` | | `stream.reset` | gap in the history | `from_seq` | ## Ordering and guarantees - Events of the same run are **ordered** by `seq`; the client must not assume they arrive exactly once — a duplicate is skipped by `id`. - `llm.chunk` is **best-effort** (it may be lost on reconnect); the full text is in the `log` artifact. After a reconnect the UI loads the last N events and continues. - No `llm.chunk` carries prompt/system messages (only the model output). ## Minimal client pseudocode ```ts const es = new EventSource(url, { withCredentials: false }); es.onmessage = (m) => apply(JSON.parse(m.data)); es.addEventListener('run.failed', (m) => showError(JSON.parse(m.data))); es.onerror = () => { /* EventSource reconnects by itself; on 401 → refresh token */ }; ``` SSE authorization goes through the `Authorization` header, so in practice `fetch` + `ReadableStream` is used (EventSource does not send headers). Reference implementation: `web/src/lib/sse.ts`.

title: API basics
text: # API basics The platform exposes a REST API for automation, integrations and reporting. The full endpoint reference is generated from the OpenAPI contract. ## Base URL | Environment | URL | |---|---| | Local | `http://localhost:18080/api/v1` | | Staging / production | your deployment URL + `/api/v1` | Every path except `/auth/*` and `/healthz` is scoped to an organisation. ## Authentication Obtain an access token, then send it as a bearer token: ```bash TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST http://localhost:18080/api/v1/auth/login \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"email":"you@company.com","password":"..."}' | jq -r .access_token) curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ http://localhost:18080/api/v1/orgs/$ORG/projects ``` Access tokens are short-lived. Refresh tokens rotate; store them in an HTTP-only cookie or a secret manager. ## Conventions - **JSON** request and response bodies. - **Pagination** with `limit` and `cursor`; the response includes `next_cursor` when more data exists. - **Idempotency** with an `Idempotency-Key` header on mutating requests; replaying the same key and body returns the original result. - **Errors** use a stable shape: `{"error":{"code":"...","message":"...","request_id":"..."}}` plus an HTTP status. - **Rate limits** return `429` with `Retry-After`; honour it. - **Versioning** is in the path (`/api/v1`); breaking changes require a new version. ## Common status codes | Code | Meaning | |---|---| | 200 / 201 | Success / created | | 202 | Accepted; a run or async job started | | 204 | No content | | 400 | Validation error | | 401 | Missing or invalid token | | 403 | Role or project access denied | | 404 | Resource not found in this organisation | | 409 | Invalid transition or idempotency conflict | | 421 | Region mismatch | | 429 | Rate limited | | 500 | Server error with a request ID | ## Live events Run events are available over server-sent events: ```text GET /api/v1/orgs/{org}/runs/{run}/events Accept: text/event-stream Last-Event-ID: 42 ``` Reconnect with the last sequence number. The event catalog describes event types and payloads. ## Webhooks Project and workspace webhooks deliver signed events for run completion, PR state and approvals. Verify the signature before processing; retries use exponential backoff. ## Next - [API reference](../api.html) — all endpoints and schemas - [SSE event catalog](api-events.html) - [Security and audit](security-audit.html)
